lesson.title: Writing Algorithms Before You Write Code
lesson.summary: Pseudocode lets you plan the logic of an algorithm in plain, structured language before you commit to any programming language's exact syntax.
lesson.body:
When you design an algorithm, the hardest part is usually figuring out the steps, not typing them into a computer. Pseudocode is a way to write those steps down using structured, English-like language, without worrying about semicolons, indentation rules, or a specific language's keywords. It sits between "an idea in your head" and "working code," and it lets you focus entirely on the logic of the algorithm you are designing.

Pseudocode borrows the shape of real code (loops, conditionals, variables) but uses plain words instead of strict syntax. A typical pseudocode statement might read IF value > max_value THEN or FOR EACH item IN list. There is no single official pseudocode standard, but good pseudocode is consistent, uses indentation to show which statements belong inside a loop or conditional, and describes one clear step at a time.

Consider the algorithm design problem of finding the largest number in a list. In pseudocode, you might write:

ALGORITHM FindMaximum(numbers)
    max_value = numbers[0]
    FOR EACH value IN numbers:
        IF value > max_value:
            max_value = value
    RETURN max_value

Notice that this says nothing about Python, Java, or any other language. It says: start by assuming the first number is the biggest, then look at every number in the list, and whenever you find one bigger than your current best, update your best. That is the algorithm. Only after this logic is solid do you translate it into a real language:

def find_maximum(numbers):
    max_value = numbers[0]
    for value in numbers:
        if value > max_value:
            max_value = value
    return max_value

print(find_maximum([3, 7, 2, 9, 4]))

Trace through it by hand: max_value starts at 3. Compare 7 to 3, 7 is bigger, so max_value becomes 7. Compare 2 to 7, no change. Compare 9 to 7, 9 is bigger, so max_value becomes 9. Compare 4 to 9, no change. The function returns 9, which is indeed the largest value in the list.

Writing pseudocode first is not busywork. It separates two different skills: designing the algorithm (the sequence of decisions and actions that solves the problem) and writing correct syntax in a particular language. When you skip straight to code, it is easy to get tangled in syntax errors while you are still unsure whether your logic is even right. Pseudocode also makes it easier to communicate an algorithm to someone else, or to your future self, since it reads almost like a numbered set of instructions rather than a specific programming language's dialect.
